response.headline: AI Weekly: OpenAI Nvidia tensions? Wild week for AI stocks

quote - 'nonsense'.Meanwhile, the Financial Times reported Nvidia's H200 AI chip sales to China are still uncertain due to a U.S. national security review.It said the U.S. State Department wants tougher restrictions.It aims to make it harder for China to use the H200 chips in ways that would undermine U.S. national security.The report added Chinese customers haven't placed orders until it's clear they can secure licenses and know what conditions will be attached.AI-related stocks went through a wild week.Tech majors like Meta, ASML and SK Hynix soared. Investors bought the Facebook-parent as it boosted spending plans by close to three quarters in pursuit of "superintelligence".That's where machines surpass human performance.But other major tech stocks like Microsoft and AMD struggled.Microsoft endured a more than 10% one day drop after AI spending worried investors.The firm only edged past forecasts for quarterly revenue on its cloud-computing business, and ramped up AI spending.That disappointed market watchers who wanted better returns amid intense competition.And Samsung forecast chip shortages will get worse this year due to the AI boom.It expects any expansion of memory chip supply to be limited over the next two years while AI-related demand stays strong.However, revenues were up big time in the fourth quarter for the world's top memory chipmaker.Operating profit at Samsung's chip business surged 470% to a record high $11.4 billion in the fourth quarter from a year earlier.

response.headline: This Is What Whales Are Betting On NVIDIA
Nvidia's China chip sales stalled by US security review: FT
response.summary: STORY: Nvidia’s H200 AI chip sales to China are in question due to a pending U.S. national security review. That’s according to the Financial Times Tuesday (February 3), citing sources. It comes almost two months after U.S. President Donald Trump approved the tech giant’s exports. Meanwhile, the report said, Chinese customers aren't placing orders for the powerful H200 chip with Nvidia. They’re waiting for clarity on whether they’ll be able to secure licenses - or the conditions that could be attached. Reuters couldn't immediately verify the report. Nvidia and the U.S. State Department didn't immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment.In January, the Commerce Department eased export curbs on the H200 for China.But it required license applications to be reviewed by the U.S. departments of State, Defense and Energy.According to the FT, the Commerce Department has completed its analysis but the State Department was pushing for tougher restrictions...With its goal being to make it harder for China to use the H200 chips in ways that would undermine U.S. national security.Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said last week his firm's license to sell the chip in the country is being finalized.Reuters reported last month that China had approved its first batch of H200 chips for import.It marks a shift for Beijing as it tries to balance its AI needs against pushing domestic development.
